subject: Physiology
summary: Hearing converts sound waves into neural signals that the brain interprets as sound. It relies on outer, middle and inner ear structures and precise neural pathways. Disruption at any level can cause hearing loss or auditory hallucinations.

sections.p: Hearing is a sensory modality that allows detection of vibrations in the air and their translation into electrical impulses for the brain.
b: Essential for communication, safety and learning
Impaired hearing affects language development and quality of life

sections.p: Sound enters the external auditory canal, vibrates the tympanic membrane, is amplified by the ossicles, and moves fluid in the cochlea where hair cells transduce motion into nerve impulses.
b: Outer ear: pinna & canal collect sound
Middle ear: ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify
Inner ear: scala vestibuli, scala tympani, basilar membrane, hair cells
Auditory nerve carries signals to brainstem and auditory cortex

t.b: What is the patient’s hearing threshold across frequencies? → Determines degree (mild‑profound) and type (conductive vs sensorineural) of loss
Is middle‑ear pressure normal? → Detects middle‑ear effusion, eustachian tube dysfunction, or ossicular discontinuity
Are outer hair cells functioning? → Absent OAEs suggest sensorineural loss; useful when audiometry unavailable

sections.p: The auditory system adapts via the acoustic reflex and central gain control, protecting the inner ear from loud sounds and maintaining sensitivity.
b: Stapedial reflex reduces ossicular movement for loud sounds
Cochlear hair cells have active amplification via outer hair cell motility

sections.p: Hearing loss can be conductive, sensorineural, or mixed, each with distinct pathophysiology and common causes, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Conductive: otitis media, cholesteatoma, tympanic perforation
Sensorineural: presbycusis, noise exposure, ototoxic drugs, meningitis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, TB meningitis, malaria‑related cerebral involvement
Mixed: combination of above

t.b: Is an infectious cause present? → Positive results guide antimicrobial therapy, crucial in endemic areas
Is there retrocochlear pathology (e.g., acoustic neuroma, TB granuloma)? → Abnormalities require neurosurgical or medical referral

sections.p: Early identification of hearing impairment prevents developmental delays, improves treatment adherence, and reduces morbidity from associated infections.
b: Unaddressed hearing loss in children → language delay, poor school performance
Adults with sudden sensorineural loss → risk of permanent deafness if untreated within 72 h

t.b: Should steroids be started? → Indicated for idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss; improves recovery if given early
Is bacterial infection likely? → Amoxicillin first‑line; prevents chronic perforation and mastoiditis

sections.p: Focus on differentiating conductive vs sensorineural loss, recognizing red‑flag symptoms, and knowing first‑line investigations.
b: Rinne test: bone > air = conductive loss
Weber test: lateralizes to affected ear in conductive loss, to better ear in sensorineural loss
Sudden unilateral loss → treat as emergency

whenToSeekHelp: Severe otalgia with facial nerve palsy

faq.q: What is the difference between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss?
faq.a: Conductive loss stems from problems in the outer/middle ear; sensorineural loss originates in the inner ear or auditory nerve.
It quantifies hearing thresholds across frequencies, allowing classification of loss severity and type.

faq.q: Can infections cause permanent hearing loss?
faq.a: Yes; meningitis, TB, and severe otitis media can damage hair cells or the auditory nerve irreversibly.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of sensorineural hearing loss and list two common causes in low‑resource settings.
Interpret Rinne and Weber test results in a patient with unilateral ear pain.
Outline the urgent management steps for sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic otologic exam differentiate conductive from sensorineural loss and identify red‑flag pathology.
b: Onset (sudden vs gradual) and duration of hearing change.
Unilateral vs bilateral involvement; any associated otalgia, otorrhea, vertigo, tinnitus or aural fullness.
Exposure history: loud noise, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, chemotherapy), HIV status, TB treatment, pregnancy, head trauma.
Developmental milestones in children; language acquisition; school performance.
Family history of early‑onset hearing loss or genetic syndromes.
Previous ear surgery, tympanostomy tubes, or chronic ear discharge.
Systemic symptoms: fever, rash, weight loss (suggesting infection or malignancy).

t.a: Inspection of external ear and canal
t.b: Detects deformities, discharge, or cerumen blockage; a normal appearance does not exclude middle‑ear disease.
Assesses tympanic membrane mobility, color, perforation, retraction pocket, cholesteatoma; cannot quantify degree of conductive loss.
Compares air‑ vs bone‑conduction; air > bone (positive) = normal or sensorineural; bone > air (negative) = conductive. Does not grade severity.
Places fork on forehead; lateralisation to affected ear suggests conductive loss, to better ear suggests sensorineural loss. Cannot differentiate mixed loss.
Helps confirm unilateral sensorineural loss when Weber lateralises to the better ear; not feasible at bedside without equipment.
Classifies middle‑ear pressure: Type A (normal), Type B (fluid or perforation), Type C (negative pressure). Absence of equipment limits assessment.
Patient repeats words at comfortable level; percentage correct estimates functional hearing. Not a precise audiometric measure.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations based on bedside findings; each test answers a specific diagnostic question.
b: When conductive loss is suspected, confirm middle‑ear status and rule out ossicular fixation.
When sensorineural loss is suspected, evaluate cochlear vs retrocochlear pathology.
In children or pregnant women, prioritize non‑invasive, radiation‑free tests.

t.b: Quantifies air‑ and bone‑conduction thresholds across frequencies; conductive loss shows air‑bone gap ≥10 dB, sensorineural loss shows parallel elevation. If unavailable, use bedside tuning‑fork comparison.
Detects outer‑hair‑cell function; absent OAEs indicate cochlear (sensorineural) loss. Normal OAEs with hearing loss suggest retrocochlear lesion.
Assesses neural conduction time; prolonged latencies point to retrocochlear (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) pathology. Normal ABR does not exclude cochlear loss.
Shows ossicular chain integrity, cholesteatoma, otosclerosis, or mastoid disease; indicated when conductive loss persists despite normal tympanometry.

t.a: MRI brain with internal auditory canal protocol
t.b: Detects vestibular schwannoma, demyelinating lesions, or central lesions causing sensorineural loss. Use when ABR abnormal or sudden unilateral loss with no middle‑ear cause.

t.a: Serum PCR for congenital CMV (urine or saliva within first 3 weeks)
t.b: Definitive test for CMV‑related sensorineural loss in infants with microcephaly and periventricular calcifications. If unavailable, rely on clinical picture and consider referral.

t.a: Serology for syphilis (RPR/VDRL) and HIV testing
t.b: Identifies infectious causes of sensorineural loss; positive result prompts antimicrobial therapy. If tests not on site, send to reference lab.
Screen for diabetic microvascular disease contributing to sensorineural loss. Manage hyperglycaemia if abnormal.

sections.p: Classification integrates audiometric thresholds, laterality, and aetiology to guide management.
b: Conductive hearing loss: air‑bone gap ≥10 dB on PTA; bone‑conduction thresholds normal (<25 dB).
Sensorineural hearing loss: air‑ and bone‑conduction thresholds parallel, both ≥25 dB.
Mixed hearing loss: air‑bone gap ≥10 dB with elevated bone thresholds.
Mild loss: 26‑40 dB; moderate: 41‑55 dB; moderately severe: 56‑70 dB; severe: 71‑90 dB; profound: >90 dB.
Sudden sensorineural loss: ≥30 dB drop in ≥3 contiguous frequencies within ≤72 h.
Presbycusis: bilateral, high‑frequency (>2 kHz) loss, gradual onset after age 60.

sections.p: Certain pathologies mimic conductive or sensorineural loss; targeted questions and tests separate them.

t.a: Otitis media with effusion vs otosclerosis
t.b: Both give conductive loss; tympanometry Type B (fluid) suggests effusion, Type A with stapedial reflex absent suggests otosclerosis.
Fluctuating low‑frequency loss, tinnitus, aural fullness point to Menière’s; vestibular migraine may have normal audiogram. MRI helps exclude retrocochlear lesions.

t.a: Retrocochlear tumour (vestibular schwannoma) vs severe sensorineural loss
t.b: ABR prolonged inter‑peak latencies or absent waves suggest tumour; normal OAEs with poor speech discrimination raise suspicion.
Both cause sensorineural loss and calcifications; CMV PCR from urine is definitive; rubella IgM may be supportive but less specific.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures rapid treatment of acute loss and long‑term care of chronic impairment.
b: 1. Confirm type of loss with tuning‑fork (Rinne, Weber) and bedside otoscopy; differentiate conductive vs sensorineural.
2. For sudden unilateral sensorineural loss (<72 h), start high‑dose oral prednisone; add oral antiviral if viral aetiology suspected.
3. If no improvement after 5‑7 days, consider intratympanic dexamethasone or methylprednisolone injection.
4. Conduct audiometry to document baseline thresholds; repeat at 1 month and then annually for chronic cases.
5. For chronic conductive loss, treat underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics for otitis media, surgical repair of perforation, ossiculoplasty).
6. Refer to otolaryngology if: persistent conductive loss >30 dB, cholesteatoma suspected, facial nerve palsy, or failed medical therapy.
7. Provide hearing rehabilitation: hearing aids for moderate‑severe sensorineural loss, bone‑anchored devices for conductive loss when surgery not feasible.
8. Counsel on ototoxic drug avoidance, noise protection, and regular follow‑up.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Steroids are first‑line for sudden sensorineural loss but have important adverse profiles.
b: Systemic prednisone: may cause hyperglycaemia, hypertension, gastric irritation; monitor blood glucose in diabetics and give proton‑pump inhibitor if ulcer risk.
Intratympanic dexamethasone: rare tympanic membrane perforation; if perforation occurs, apply topical antibiotic and refer for repair.
Aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin) used for severe otitis media: risk of irreversible sensorineural loss; avoid in patients with existing hearing impairment.
Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) can precipitate acute cochlear toxicity; ensure serum electrolytes are normal and use lowest effective dose.
Antiretroviral drugs (e.g., didanosine) have reported ototoxicity; monitor audiogram annually in HIV patients on these agents.

sections.p: Recognise red‑flag features that demand urgent specialist input.
b: Progressive conductive loss with foul‑smelling otorrhoea and retraction pocket → suspect cholesteatoma; arrange CT temporal bone and urgent ENT review.
Sudden sensorineural loss >30 dB across three frequencies persisting >7 days despite steroids → consider retrocochlear pathology; order MRI brain with contrast.
Persistent vertigo, facial nerve weakness, or severe tinnitus with hearing loss → possible labyrinthine fistula; avoid Valsalva, refer immediately.
Rapidly worsening hearing in pregnancy with negative Rinne bilaterally → suspect otosclerosis; arrange audiometry and consider referral for stapedectomy after delivery.
Uncontrolled HIV with opportunistic ear infections leading to mixed loss → start appropriate antimicrobial therapy and refer for audiologic rehabilitation.

sections.p: Various systemic conditions modify presentation, investigations, and treatment choices.
b: HIV: higher rates of chronic otitis media, CMV‑related sensorineural loss; PCR from urine or saliva is definitive for congenital CMV, not IgM alone.
TB meningitis can cause bilateral sensorineural loss; CSF analysis and GeneXpert guide anti‑TB therapy.
Malnutrition lowers serum albumin, affecting middle‑ear pressure regulation; treat nutritional deficiency alongside infection.
Pregnancy increases vascularity of the stapes footplate, worsening otosclerosis; avoid ototoxic drugs and defer surgery until postpartum.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens steroid‑induced glucose spikes; monitor glucose closely when prescribing oral prednisone.
Herbal remedies containing aristolochic acid or high‑dose quinine can be ototoxic; obtain a thorough medication history.
Renal failure impairs clearance of aminoglycosides; dose‑adjust or avoid these agents.
Advanced age: presbycusis common; differentiate from treatable conductive components before fitting hearing aids.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy to the patient’s context and resources.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate audiometry (visual reinforcement audiometry, ABR); avoid ototoxic antibiotics; schedule hearing aid fitting before language milestones are missed.
Pregnancy: prioritize oral steroids over intratympanic injections; counsel on noise avoidance; defer elective middle‑ear surgery until after delivery.
Elderly: screen for presbycusis with pure‑tone audiometry; consider cognitive status before hearing‑aid training; monitor for steroid‑induced hypertension.
People with HIV: perform PCR for CMV in congenital cases; screen for opportunistic ear infections; coordinate with infectious disease team for drug interactions.
Low‑resource settings: use portable audiometer or smartphone‑based hearing test; treat otitis media with oral amoxicillin; refer for hearing aid donation programmes when needed.

sections.p: Sample questions to test mastery of the deep notes.

t.a: Describe the step‑by‑step bedside technique for Rinne and Weber tests and interpret a negative Rinne with Weber laterali
t.b: Rinne: place 512 Hz fork on mastoid, wait for fade, then near canal; compare air vs bone. Negative Rinne means bone > air → conductive loss. Weber lateralising to right indicates conductive loss in right ear.

t.a: A pregnant woman has bilateral conductive loss and a stiff ‘As’ tympanogram. What is the most likely structural abnormal
t.b: Stapes footplate fixation (otosclerosis) causing reduced compliance; confirmed by absent stapedial reflex.

t.a: List two common causes of sensorineural loss in low‑resource hospitals and the pathophysiologic mechanism for each.
t.b: Presbycusis – age‑related loss of hair‑cell function; Noise exposure – mechanical damage to outer hair cells and synaptic loss.

t.a: What is the definitive laboratory test for congenital CMV infection causing microcephaly and hearing loss?
t.b: PCR detection of CMV DNA from urine or saliva collected within the first three weeks of life.

t.a: Outline the monitoring schedule for a patient with chronic sensorineural loss after initial treatment.
t.b: Audiogram at 1 month, then annually; review ototoxic drug exposure and renal function each visit.

t.a: A patient on gentamicin develops new tinnitus and high‑frequency loss. What immediate action is required?
t.b: Stop gentamicin, obtain baseline audiogram, consider alternative antibiotic, and monitor renal function.

t.a: Explain why ABR latency alone does not differentiate conductive from sensorineural loss.
t.b: ABR latency may be normal in cochlear loss but prolonged in retrocochlear lesions; it does not reflect middle‑ear conduction.

t.a: When should intratympanic steroids be considered for sudden sensorineural loss?
t.b: If oral steroids fail to improve hearing after 5‑7 days, or if contraindications to systemic steroids exist.

t.a: Identify the histopathological hallmark of Ménière’s disease.
t.b: Endolymphatic hydrops – distended scala media with ruptured Reissner’s membrane.

t.a: What screening protocol is recommended for hearing in well‑child visits up to age 5?
t.b: Otoacoustic emissions or automated ABR at newborn, then age‑appropriate pure‑tone screening at 9 months, 18 months, and annually thereafter.

facts: Normal air‑bone gap ≤10 dB across frequencies indicates no conductive loss.
Sensorineural loss: air‑ and bone‑conduction thresholds parallel, both ≥30 dB.
Conductive loss: bone‑conduction better than air‑conduction by ≥15 dB (positive Rinne).
Presbycusis typically begins >60 years with high‑frequency loss >2 kHz.
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is defined as ≥30 dB loss in ≥3 contiguous frequencies within 72 h.
Intratympanic steroids are considered if oral therapy fails after 7‑10 days.
Annual audiometry is recommended for chronic sensorineural loss monitoring.
Weber lateralises to the side of conductive loss, to the better ear in sensorineural loss.
Acoustic reflex threshold >100 dB SPL suggests severe cochlear damage.

vivas.q: Define conductive hearing loss and give two common low‑resource causes.
vivas.a: Conductive loss is reduced air‑conduction with normal bone‑conduction; common causes are chronic otitis media with effusion and tympanic membrane perforation.

vivas.q: What bedside steps are required for a Rinne test and how do you interpret a negative result?
vivas.a: Place 512 Hz fork on mastoid until sound fades, then near the ear canal; if bone > air (negative Rinne) it indicates conductive loss on that side.

vivas.q: Explain why the Weber test lateralises to the affected ear in conductive loss.
vivas.a: The conductive ear conducts bone vibration more efficiently, so the patient perceives the tone louder on that side.

vivas.q: A pregnant woman has bilateral conductive loss with negative Rinne bilaterally. What structural abnormality explains this?
vivas.a: Hormone‑induced mucosal edema of the Eustachian tube leading to middle‑ear effusion (otitis media with effusion).

vivas.q: What is the most definitive laboratory test for congenital CMV causing microcephaly and sensorineural loss?
vivas.a: PCR detection of CMV DNA from urine or saliva collected within the first three weeks of life.

vivas.q: List the urgent management steps for sudden unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
vivas.a: Start high‑dose oral prednisone within 2 weeks, counsel on avoiding ototoxic drugs, arrange audiometry, consider intratympanic steroids if no improvement after 7‑10 days.

vivas.q: Why is ABR latency not a reliable sole marker of sensorineural loss?
vivas.a: ABR may be normal in cochlear loss but prolonged or absent in retrocochlear pathology; thresholds and OAEs give a fuller picture.

vivas.q: Describe the acoustic reflex and its clinical relevance.
vivas.a: Stapedial muscle contracts in response to loud sounds, reducing ossicular movement; absent reflex suggests severe cochlear loss or facial nerve lesion.
Endolymphatic hydrops – distended Reissner’s membrane with excess endolymph in the scala media.

vivas.q: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media shows a deep retraction pocket. What pathology is expected on microscopy?
vivas.a: Squamous epithelium with keratin debris and possible cholesteatoma formation.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the presentation of sensorineural hearing loss?
vivas.a: HIV can cause opportunistic infections (CMV, syphilis) and ototoxic antiretrovirals, leading to rapid, bilateral loss often at higher frequencies.

vivas.q: When tympanometry shows a stiff ‘As’ curve and absent stapedial reflex, what diagnosis is most likely?
What are the key history questions for a child with suspected hearing loss?
vivas.a: Ask about delayed speech, noisy environment, recurrent otitis media, family history of deafness, exposure to ototoxic drugs, and maternal infections during pregnancy.

vivas.q: Why should intratympanic steroids not be given within the first 48 h of sudden loss?
vivas.a: Early oral steroids are more effective; premature intratympanic injection adds procedural risk without proven benefit.

vivas.q: What is the recommended frequency of audiometric monitoring for chronic sensorineural loss?
vivas.a: Annually, unless there is a change in symptoms or exposure to ototoxic agents.

vivas.q: Explain the difference between OAEs and ABR in evaluating hearing loss.
vivas.a: OAEs assess outer‑hair‑cell function and are absent in cochlear loss; ABR evaluates neural conduction and can detect retrocochlear lesions.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot differentiate between sensorineural and central auditory pathway lesions?
vivas.a: Weber test alone; it lateralises but does not identify retrocochlear versus central pathology.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource setting without audiometry, how can you screen for conductive loss?
vivas.a: Use tuning‑fork tests (Rinne and Weber) and otoscopic inspection for tympanic membrane abnormalities.

mcqs.q: A 28‑year‑old woman in her third trimester reports progressive hearing loss. Tuning‑fork testing shows a negative Rinne bilaterally. Which is the most likely cause?
mcqs.e: Pregnancy hormones cause Eustachian tube edema leading to conductive loss.

mcqs.q: Which test is definitive for confirming congenital CMV infection in a newborn with microcephaly and hearing loss?
mcqs.e: PCR of urine or saliva is the gold standard for congenital CMV.

mcqs.q: A patient presents with unilateral sudden SNHL, tinnitus and aural fullness. Which management step is first?
mcqs.e: Oral prednisone started within 2 weeks is first‑line.

mcqs.q: Tympanometry shows a shallow ‘Ad’ curve. What does this indicate?
mcqs.e: ‘Ad’ denotes a highly compliant system, typical of ossicular discontinuity or tympanic membrane perforation.

mcqs.q: Which histopathological finding is characteristic of Menière’s disease?
mcqs.e: Distended Reissner’s membrane reflects endolymphatic hydrops.

mcqs.q: A child with chronic otitis media has a deep retraction pocket. What is the most likely complication?
mcqs.e: Retraction pockets can accumulate keratin and evolve into cholesteatoma.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of sensorineural hearing loss in low‑resource settings?
mcqs.e: Cerumen impaction causes conductive, not sensorineural loss.

mcqs.q: During a Weber test, the tone is heard louder in the left ear. The Rinne test is positive on the left and negative on the right. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Weber lateralises to the right (conductive ear); right Rinne negative confirms right conductive loss.

cases.v: A 5‑year‑old boy is brought by his mother because he does not respond to her name and repeats words slowly. No history of ear discharge. Otoscopy shows a normal tympanic membrane. Tuning‑fork testing: Rinne positive bilaterally, Weber lateralises to the right.

qs.q: What type of hearing loss is most likely?
qs.a: Sensorineural loss in the right ear (Weber lateralises to the better ear).

qs.q: Which investigation should be arranged first?
qs.a: Pure‑tone audiometry with bone‑conduction thresholds, followed by OAE to assess outer‑hair‑cell function.

qs.q: What is the initial management step?
qs.a: Refer for audiological rehabilitation and speech therapy; screen for possible congenital infections and ototoxic drug exposure.

mistakes: Confusing a negative Rinne (bone > air) as sensorineural rather than conductive.
Assuming ABR latency normality rules out sensorineural loss; retrocochlear lesions alter ABR.
Giving intratympanic steroids within 48 h of sudden loss instead of starting oral steroids first.
Monitoring chronic sensorineural loss every 4‑6 weeks; guidelines recommend annual review.
Using IgM serology alone to diagnose congenital CMV; PCR from urine/saliva is definitive.
Interpreting a Weber lateralising to the affected ear as sensorineural rather than conductive.
Failing to consider pregnancy‑related middle‑ear effusion as a cause of conductive loss.
Neglecting to screen for ototoxic drug exposure when evaluating progressive SNHL.
